caption:
14% of employees find the appraisal process motivating. The rest sit through it. Senior leadership is tracking around 8.5% increments while juniors see more, against an India average near 8.9%. Engagement sits at 23%. Expected attrition, 13.6%.

Read that properly. The machinery that is supposed to recognise you is not built to notice you. It is built to distribute a budget.

So you argue your own case. Not with resentment, not with a long email. With a prepared position.

Three things before you walk into a calibration conversation:

One. Know your number before they say theirs. A leader who has not decided his own figure will accept whichever one is offered.

Two. Bring evidence, not effort. Outcomes with dates attached. Hours worked are not an argument.

Three. State it once, then hold the silence. Most people lose the room by filling the pause with concessions nobody asked for.

November is case-building season. Build the case.

topic.title: Only 14% find appraisals motivating — argue your own case
topic.angle: This turns "qualified but overlooked" from a feeling into a statistic for an audience whose formal recognition machinery demonstrably fails them — with senior leadership getting smaller percentage increments (around 8.5%) than juniors.
topic.why_now: Late October through November is when India's mid-cycle reviews, calibration conversations and promotion-case-building happen before the main cycle lands, and the 2026 numbers (8.9% average hike, 13.6% expected attrition, 23% engagement) were compiled roughly 13 days ago.

rationale: A stark, text-only statistic card matches the no-nonsense tone and lets the 14% figure carry the post without decoration.
